questions.question: A container log shows the main process exited with status 137. What does that most likely mean?
options: The process received SIGTERM and shut down gracefully
The process was killed by SIGKILL (128 + 9), often by the out-of-memory killer
questions.explanation: When a signal kills a process the shell reports 128 plus the signal number. 137 is 128 + 9 (SIGKILL); 143 would be SIGTERM.

questions.question: Why should you send SIGTERM before resorting to `kill -9`?
options: SIGTERM can be caught, letting the program finish work, flush data and clean up; SIGKILL cannot
SIGKILL only works for processes owned by root
questions.explanation: SIGTERM is a polite request a program can handle to shut down cleanly. SIGKILL ends the process immediately and cannot be caught, risking corrupted or half-written data.

questions.question: You started a long command in the foreground and pressed Ctrl+Z. How do you let it continue running in the background?
questions.explanation: Ctrl+Z sends SIGTSTP and stops the job. bg resumes the current stopped job in the background; fg would bring it back to the foreground.

questions.question: What is a zombie process?
options: A process stuck waiting on disk I/O
A running process whose parent has exited
A process that has exited but whose parent has not yet collected its exit status with wait
A process running with the lowest nice value
questions.explanation: A zombie (state Z) has finished but still holds a process-table entry until its parent reaps it. A running process whose parent exited is an orphan, adopted by PID 1.
